methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Dual Component (Math + ELA) Project
content: Problem: Students have learned isolated math concepts (addition, measurement, shapes) but struggle to synthesize them into a continuous, comprehensive presentation.

Solution: This week is a Project Week ("My Math Museum"). Students will use the Dual Component structure to design specific museum "exhibits." Part 1 (Math Component) reviews the hard math logic and vocabulary for each exhibit. Part 2 & 3 (ELA Component) provides the descriptive and sequence language needed to guide a visitor through the museum.

parts.title: PART 1: MATH COMPONENT (Reading & Vocab)
content: A. Math Reading Input: The Operations Exhibit
Today, you are the curator (người quản lý) of your own Math Museum!
Your first job is to build the Operations Exhibit.
"We must show addition and subtraction," says Detective Max.
Addition makes things bigger. You combine two groups. For example, ten plus (cộng) five equals (bằng) fifteen.
Subtraction makes things smaller. You take things away. For example, fifteen minus (trừ) five equals ten.
Visitors will learn that addition and subtraction are exact opposites.
Let's build a beautiful museum (bảo tàng) for everyone to see!
Note: Because this is a review week, show your mastery directly!
b. I know that ten _______________ ten is twenty.
b. A big number _______________ a small number.
b. The two sides must _______________ each other.

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT (Reading & Vocab)
content: A. ELA Reading Input: Guiding the Visitors
To be a great museum guide, you must use clear sequence words.
"First, welcome the visitors to the museum," says Max. "Tell them what they will see."
"Next, point to the addition exhibit. Explain how numbers get bigger."
"Then, walk to the subtraction room. Show them how to take numbers away."
Using words like 'First', 'Next', and 'Then' helps visitors understand your math story perfectly.

content: A. Math Reading Input: Shapes and Patterns
Next, we must build the Geometry Gallery in our museum!
"We must show shapes (hình khối) and patterns (quy luật)," says Detective Luna.
A shape like a square has four equal straight sides and four corners. A triangle has three sides.
A pattern is a rule that repeats. If we put a square, then a triangle, then a square, we have a pattern!
The rule is: repeat square, then triangle.
Geometry helps us see the beautiful logic in the world around us.
a. A triangle is a strong _______________.

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT (Reading & Vocab)
content: A. ELA Reading Input: Describing the Geometry Gallery
As a tour guide, Luna writes her speech for the new gallery.
"After that, we walk into the beautiful Geometry Gallery. Look at the shapes!"
"A square has four straight sides, but a circle is perfectly round."
"Then, look at the pattern on the wall. A pattern is a rule that always repeats."
Using contrast words like 'but' helps visitors compare different shapes easily.
a. A square is flat, _______________ a ball is round.
b. I like math, _______________ it is hard.

content: A. Math Reading Input: Measurement & Place Value
Finally, we build the Measurement and Place Value Exhibits!
"We must measure (đo lường) things," says Pip.
We use a ruler to measure length (chiều dài). The board is fifty centimeters long.
We use a scale to measure weight (cân nặng). The stone is very heavy.

Measurement and place value give us exact information to solve problems!
b. Use a ruler to _______________ it.

parts.title: PART 2: ELA COMPONENT (Reading & Vocab)
content: A. ELA Reading Input: The Grand Finale
The museum is almost finished! You write the final speech.
"Finally, we arrive at the Measurement Lab. Here, we must be exact!"

"As you can see, math is everywhere. Thank you for visiting our complete Math Museum!"
A great presentation uses strong concluding sentences.
a. The _______________ of the stone is big.
b. I check the _______________ on the scale.
